newsitem.title: CHINA: China activists shelve anti-Japan embassy protest.
newsitem.headline: China activists shelve anti-Japan embassy protest.

text.p: Chinese anti-Japan activists on Friday shelved plans for a demonstration in Beijing to protest Tokyo's control over a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea, a leading campaigner said.

The activists, who had come under pressure from officials to call off the protest and tone down their demands for military action over the islands, had yet to decide how they would continue their campaign, organiser Tong Zeng said.

Failure to register the planned demonstration, to be held outside the Japanese Embassy, meant it could not now be held on the September 18 anniversary of the 1931 start of the Sino-Japanese war, Tong said by telephone.
"Because we couldn't go to register today...it will be impossible to demonstrate on September 18," Tong said.

A simmering dispute over the islands, which China calls the Diaoyus and Japan the Senkakus, flared in July after a rightist Japanese group built a lighthouse on one of the uninhabited but potentially resource-rich islands.
Foreign reporters in Beijing were left waiting after Tong failed to turn up to register the embassy protest with police on Friday -- the required five days before the event.
Tong, who on Thursday said he had been pressured by officials of China's Ministry of Civil Affairs to leave Beijing, said he had been talked out of registering by a colleague from his work unit.
"He said there was now a need to look at the big picture, because there must be stability in the country," Tong said.
The Beijing activists would consider other protest strategies while waiting for a future opportunity to demonstrate, he said.

Outrage over Japan's refusal to tear down the Diaoyu lighthouse has united nationalist sentiment in Beijing as well as in arch-rival Taiwan. Even democratic activists in Hong Kong have joined calls for tough action by China.

Beijing's Communist Party-controlled media quickly condemns any perceived signs of resurgent Japanese militarism, but China has in the past suppressed unofficial protests against Tokyo and campaigns for Japanese compensation for war victims.

Tong's high-profile, anti-Japanese campaigns led authorities to confiscate his passport and exile him temporarily from Beijing during the U.N.-sponsored World Conference on Women in September last year.
